chunks: How a buck converter ages. The question: How does a buck converter age? What happens to its performance?
A buck converter slowly wears out, and the weakest part is usually the electrolytic capacitor. Its liquid evaporates, so its capacitance falls and its internal resistance rises.
The result is more ripple, a slower recovery from sudden load changes, and more heat.
Other parts age too, but slower: solder joints crack from temperature cycling, and inductor insulation weakens with heat.
Think of a cup with a slow leak. Each day a bit of liquid escapes, and the hotter the room, the faster it goes. Eventually the cup holds too little to do its job.
The electrolytic capacitor is that cup, and heat is what speeds the leak.
The picture is simpler than real life, since ceramic capacitors do not leak this way but can crack from board flex.
Early failures (assembly defects, weak parts) decline, a long flat region of random failures follows, then wear-out mechanisms (electrolytic capacitors, solder fatigue) take over.
Burn-in removes infant mortality; derating pushes the wear-out part of the curve to the right. The shape here is generic, not measured data.
Electrolytic capacitor: a capacitor with a liquid inside, which can dry out over time. ESR: the capacitor's internal series resistance, which rises as it ages.
10 degrees Celsius rule: for electrolytics, life roughly doubles for every 10 degrees Celsius cooler.
Thermal cycling: repeated heating and cooling, which fatigues solder joints and the tiny wires inside chips.
Derating: using a part well below its rated limits ("Spec the buck inductor and capacitors").
Say an electrolytic capacitor is rated for 2000 hours at 105 degrees Celsius.
If it runs at 65 degrees Celsius, that is 40 degrees Celsius cooler, which is four doublings: 2 to the 4 equals 16 .
Its expected life is about 2000 times 16 equals 32 000 hours, or nearly 3. 7 years of nonstop use. That is the whole idea.
"The weak link is the electrolytic capacitor: electrolyte evaporates, so ESR rises and capacitance falls, and life halves for every 10 degrees Celsius of heating.
That raises ripple and droop and shifts the loop. Ceramics lose a few percent capacitance per decade of time and can crack.
Inductors age through insulation and core heating; silicon and solder suffer thermal-cycling fatigue that raises thermal resistance and R DS(on) .
The converter ends up with more ripple, lower efficiency and less margin, and I design with derating and polymer/ceramic parts and test with accelerated life."
